# Putting Down the Burden

*SN 22.22, the Bhāra Sutta — set 4, Not-Self and Dependent Arising*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 2 min · 301 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This short text asks you to picture your whole experience as a load you are
carrying.

The load is the five *clung-to heaps*: form, felt experience, recognition,
putting-together activities and knowing, when they are taken personally. The
one carrying it is simply the person, called here by name and clan. Picking
the load up is *ignorant wanting*, and putting it down is that wanting fading
and ending.

If you have read the four noble truths, you will recognize the last two
answers: they are the same words, about the origin and the quenching of
dissatisfaction. The image says what those truths mean in practice. The
weight is not life itself; it is the taking up.

The closing verses add one more thing. Putting the burden down does not mean
picking up a different one, and the wanting is pulled out by the root, not
just set aside for a while.

## Translation

### The Setting

At Sāvatthī, the Buddha said:

"Bhikkhus, I will teach you the burden, the carrier of the burden, the taking
up of the burden, and the putting down of the burden. Listen.

### The Burden

"And what, bhikkhus, is the burden? It should be said: the five clung-to
heaps. Which five?

- the form clung-to heap
- the felt-experience clung-to heap
- the recognition clung-to heap
- the putting-together-activities clung-to heap
- the knowing clung-to heap

This, bhikkhus, is called the burden.

### The Carrier of the Burden

"And what, bhikkhus, is the carrier of the burden? It should be said: the
individual, this venerable one of such a name and such a clan. This,
bhikkhus, is called the carrier of the burden.

### Taking Up the Burden

"And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? It is that ignorant
wanting that leads to renewed becoming, accompanied by relishing and passion,
delighting here and there. That is:

- ignorant wanting for sensuality
- ignorant wanting for becoming
- ignorant wanting for non-becoming

This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden.

### Putting Down the Burden

"And what, bhikkhus, is the putting down of the burden? It is the complete
fading and quenching of that very ignorant wanting: giving it up,
relinquishing it, freedom, non-attachment. This, bhikkhus, is called the
putting down of the burden."

That is what the Buddha said. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, went
on to say:

### Verses

"The five heaps are indeed a burden,
and the individual is the carrier of the burden.
Taking up the burden is dissatisfaction in the world;
putting the burden down is satisfaction.

Having put the heavy burden down
and taken up no other,
having pulled out ignorant wanting together with its root,
they are free of hunger and have reached complete quenching."

The first discourse is finished.

<summary>Words used in this translation (14)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>becoming</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;bhava&quot; -- the settling of experience into a way of being that feels like somebody being something. Often translated &quot;existence.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>burden</dfn></dt>
<dd>The five clung-to heaps pictured as a load: experience taken personally. Ignorant wanting picks it up; someone who has laid down the burden no longer takes it up.</dd>
<dt><dfn>clung-to heaps</dfn></dt>
<dd>The five categories experience gets sorted into and then grasped as &quot;me&quot; or &quot;mine&quot; -- body, feeling, recognition, mental activity, and awareness. Not clinging to the categories themselves, but to the sense of ownership placed on top of them.</dd>
<dt><dfn>complete quenching</dfn></dt>
<dd>The complete going out of greed, aversion, and delusion. In AN 3.69 and SN 1.1 it describes what is reached while alive, not death.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dissatisfaction</dfn></dt>
<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>
<dt><dfn>fading</dfn></dt>
<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>
<dt><dfn>form</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;rūpa&quot; -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>heaps</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;khandhā&quot; (usually translated &quot;aggregates&quot;) -- the five piles experience gets sorted into: form, felt experience, recognition, putting-together activities, and knowing.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ignorant wanting</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;taṇhā&quot; (often translated &quot;craving&quot;), chosen to keep visible that the wanting in question is driven by not seeing clearly, not just ordinary desire.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>quenching</dfn></dt>
<dd>An extinguishing image for dissatisfaction and its causes going out. Different Pali words use this image on different pages, so the exact scope comes from the sentence.</dd>
<dt><dfn>recognition</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saññā&quot; (often translated &quot;perception&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.</dd>
<dt><dfn>world</dfn></dt>
<dd>A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world built through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense is meant.</dd>
